paras: The killing of 'Uncle A.' Finney was the shooting of an elderly Black man, described as a former slave over ninety years old, at the door of his mountain cabin in Franklin County, Virginia, in early September 1903. Three men called him to his door at night and shot him, reportedly because neighbors believed he was a sorcerer who had cast a spell on a sick woman. A son of the sick woman was arrested and released for want of evidence, and a Fredericksburg paper denounced the killing as "barbarism" and a disgrace to Virginia.

Finney lived in a cabin on the farm of the late James Martin, on Nicholson creek not far from the Patrick County line. A dispatch to the Washington Evening Star described him as "a trapper of considerable note" who hunted and did occasional chores for white people of the neighborhood. According to the same dispatch, "ignorant white people" in the vicinity and many Black residents of the county, whom it called "darkies," regarded him as a sorcerer. A New York Tribune correspondent later called him a well-known "conjuror" whom hundreds of white and Black people consulted.

Some weeks before the killing, Mrs. Mary Holley fell ill, and her illness baffled the local physicians. Rumor held that Finney had cast a spell over her, and the Alexandria Gazette reported that the belief soon "became general among the ignorant people of the neighborhood."

A few nights before September 10, three men described as "unknown" called Finney to the door of his cabin and shot him to death. The Evening Star's dispatch said shotguns and rifles were used: one shot passed through his head and killed him instantly, another tore away his right jaw, and a third passed through his neck. The Alexandria Gazette added that his hunting gun was taken.

The Evening Star's dispatch, sent from Richmond on news received from Roanoke, reported that one arrest had been made. The Alexandria Gazette identified the person arrested as a son of Mrs. Holley, held on suspicion and then dismissed for want of evidence. The same report said Mrs. Holley began to mend after Finney's death, which neighbors attributed to his killing, and that the people of Franklin County were "much stirred up" and further arrests were probable. The coverage does not name the son and reports no inquest, indictment or trial.

The killing appeared only in white papers, first as a short Richmond wire of September 10 headed "Aged Negro Shot Down" in the New York Evening World and "Shot for a Sorcerer" in the Topeka State Journal; the Washington Times and San Francisco Call ran it the next day. Two papers near Virginia carried fuller versions: the Evening Star, under the headline "Charged with Sorcery," called it "a horrible tragedy" and described the wounds, the Holley illness and the arrest, while the Alexandria Gazette added the son's release and Mrs. Holley's recovery.

The Fredericksburg Free Lance devoted an editorial, "Barbarism in Virginia," to the case. It called the killing an "atrocious murder" of a man who had committed no crime, insisted that he was shot "by white men, and these white men were Virginians," and blamed "the ignorant whites in his section" for the belief in sorcery. The editorial cast Finney as a reminder of the generation of enslaved people that had "endeared itself to the South," and it welcomed the prospect that the killers would meet "their just reward—at the end of a rope."

In October, a New York Tribune item headed "Believe in Signs" circulated in Colorado weeklies, citing Finney's death as an example of superstitions that lingered among white and Black people along the southern Atlantic coast.

Accounts differed on Mary Holley: the Alexandria Gazette called her "a white woman" who recovered after Finney's death, while the Tribune correspondent called her "a negress" whose illness "had caused her death"; the Gazette's dispatch concerned the neighborhood itself, while the Tribune item was a general piece on superstition written from Crisfield, Maryland. Only the Free Lance stated the race of the killers; the wire reports called them "three unknown men."

reader.title: Killing of 'Uncle A.' Finney
bases: Three men called an elderly Black man to his cabin door at night and shot him dead because neighbors believed he had bewitched a sick woman (A1, A3, A5).

Three men killed Finney without any legal authority, as punishment for a spell he was rumored to have cast on a sick woman (A1, A3, A5); the killers were never identified, the motive rests on neighborhood rumor, and only one editorial calls them white (A13), so the case is a probable rather than certain lynching.

Separate Richmond dispatches in the Evening Star and the Alexandria Gazette, the short wire (A1), a Virginia editorial (A13) and a later New York Tribune correspondent (A14) agree that Finney was called to his door and shot by men who thought him a sorcerer (A3, A5).

accounts.label: Short Richmond wire
accounts.gist: Finney, an ex-slave over ninety regarded as a sorcerer, was called to his door a few nights earlier by three men and shot to death.

accounts.label: Fuller Richmond dispatch (from Roanoke)
accounts.gist: Gives the place, the weapons and wounds, the rumor that he bewitched the ailing Mrs. Holley, and one arrest; the Alexandria version adds that her son was arrested and released and that she recovered.

accounts.label: Virginia editorial
accounts.gist: White Virginians who believed him a sorcerer murdered an innocent old man; the better people of the county would see them hanged.

accounts.label: New York Tribune correspondent at Crisfield, Md.
accounts.gist: Finney, a well-known conjuror, was riddled with buckshot by men who believed he had cast a spell on 'a negress named Mary Holley' that caused her death.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Aged Negro Shot Down', 'Shot for a Sorcerer' and 'Called a Sorcerer and Shot to Death' blamed 'ignorant people' and gave no comment.
The Evening Star's 'Charged with Sorcery' called it 'a horrible tragedy' and blamed belief among 'ignorant white people' and 'county darkies'.
The Free Lance's 'Barbarism in Virginia' called it an 'atrocious murder' shaming every Virginian, in paternalist terms, and welcomed hanging for the killers.
The Tribune's 'Believe in Signs' used the killing as an instance of regional superstition among whites and Blacks.

conflicts.note: The Alexandria Gazette's version comes from the Virginia dispatch about the neighborhood; the Tribune item was written from Crisfield, Md., as a general piece on superstition and is the weaker source on details.

her illness had caused her death

conflicts.note: The local dispatch (A5) is more specific and nearer in time than the later Tribune item.
Not a contradiction, but only the editorial states their race; the arrest of Mrs. Holley's son, described as the son of a white woman in A5, is consistent with it.
A4 is evidently a misprint of the same wire text.
